Likelihood ratio tests for gcTMB models

Source: R/anova.R
anova.gcTMB.Rd

Compares two or more models fitted to the same data by likelihood ratio tests, e.g. a model with and without covariates in fform, with and without random effects, or a poisson and a negative binomial model. The test assumes nested models; the growth models (logistic, gompertz, hill, weibull) are not nested, and are better compared by their AIC.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
anova(
  object,
  ...,
  test = c("LR", "F", "boot"),
  nsim = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  progress = interactive()
)

Arguments

object

A gcTMB object, the result of gcTMB.

...

Further gcTMB objects, fitted to the same data.

test

Character string. "LR" (default) for likelihood ratio tests, "F" for F-tests of gaussian or lognormal models without random effects, or "boot" for parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio tests. "Chisq", the name in earlier versions and in stats::anova, is accepted for "LR".

nsim

Integer. Number of simulations for test="boot"

seed

Integer or NULL. An optional seed for the random number generator, for test="boot"

progress

Logical. Show a progress bar for test="boot"

Value

a data frame of class anova with the number of parameters (npar), AIC, BIC, log-likelihood and deviance (minus twice the log-likelihood) of each model, and the likelihood ratio statistic (LR), its degrees of freedom (Df) and p-value (Pr(>LR)) for the comparison with the previous model. For test="F", the residual degrees of freedom (Res.Df) and residual sum of squares (RSS) instead of the deviance, and the F statistic (F) and its p-value (Pr(>F)). For test="boot", additionally the bootstrap p-value (Pr(boot)), with the simulated likelihood ratio statistics of each comparison in the attribute "boot".

Details

The models are ordered by their number of parameters, and each model is compared with the previous one: the likelihood ratio statistic is twice the difference of their log-likelihoods (the Laplace approximation of the marginal log-likelihoods for models with random effects), with the difference in the number of parameters as degrees of freedom. The test assumes that the smaller model is nested in the larger one, which is not checked. For parameters on the boundary of their range under the smaller model, e.g. a standard deviation of random effects of zero, or an infinite size of the negative binomial for the poisson model, the chi-square distribution is conservative: the p-value is approximately twice the correct value for a single standard deviation.

The tests are those of anova of nlme for models fitted with method="ML", in the layout of anova of lme4; as gcTMB fits by maximum likelihood, models with different fixed effects can be compared (REML fits of nlme cannot).

For gaussian and lognormal (on the log scale) models without random effects, test="F" gives F-tests, as nls does for continuous responses: the reduction of the (weighted) residual sum of squares per additional parameter, divided by the residual mean square of the largest model, with n - p residual degrees of freedom for p coefficients b1-b5. The F-test is exact for linear models and accounts for the estimation of the residual variance, which the likelihood ratio test does not, so it is usually preferable for small experiments.

test="boot" gives parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio tests, as PBmodcomp of the package pbkrtest: for each comparison, nsim responses are simulated from the smaller model, with new random effects, both models are fitted to each of them, and the p-value Pr(boot) is the proportion of the simulated likelihood ratio statistics at least as large as the observed one, (1 + #{LR* >= LR}) / (1 + nsim). It does not rely on the chi-square distribution, which is only approximate in small samples, for parameters on the boundary (standard deviations of random effects of zero, the poisson model within the negative binomial), and for parameters that are not identified under the smaller model (e.g. the correlation of random effects whose standard deviation is zero under the smaller model). The chi-square p-value is shown for comparison. Each model is fitted twice to each simulated response, starting at its estimates and at the starting values of gcTMB, and the better fit is used; simulations without a finite log-likelihood of both models are left out.

Examples

FabaHeights25$trt <- factor(FabaHeights25$Treatment)
fit0 <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, data=FabaHeights25)
fit1 <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, fform=b1 ~ trt, data=FabaHeights25)
anova(fit0, fit1)
#> Likelihood ratio tests of gcTMB models
#> 
#>      npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance     LR Df  Pr(>LR)   
#> fit0    4 1406.5 1419.7 -699.23   1398.5                      
#> fit1    8 1396.2 1422.6 -690.10   1380.2 18.262  4 0.001097 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
anova(fit0, fit1, test="F")
#> F-tests of gcTMB models
#> 
#>      npar    AIC    BIC  logLik Res.Df   RSS     F Df   Pr(>F)   
#> fit0    4 1406.5 1419.7 -699.23    197 12744                     
#> fit1    8 1396.2 1422.6 -690.10    193 11632 4.613  4 0.001404 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
# random effects of the plants
fit2 <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, fform=b1 ~ trt, rform=b1 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data=FabaHeights25)
anova(fit1, fit2)
#> Likelihood ratio tests of gcTMB models
#> 
#>      npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance     LR Df   Pr(>LR)    
#> fit1    8 1396.2 1422.6 -690.10   1380.2                        
#> fit2    9 1134.2 1163.9 -558.09   1116.2 264.02  1 < 2.2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
